title: Scene, units and axes
sub: Why a model arrives 1000 times too big, or lying on its side
cards/0/title: A file often holds a whole scene
cards/0/body:
A file stores not one mesh but a tree of objects: car → body → four wheels. Each node has its own transform: translation, rotation and scale relative to its parent.

Rotate the car, and the wheels go with it.
cards/1/q: Arrange the hierarchy from top to bottom
cards/1/explain: The wheel is a child of the body, the body is a child of the car, the car is a child of the scene.
cards/2/body:
The number 10 in a file: 10 of what? By spec, glTF is always in meters. FBX stores the scale in the file settings. OBJ and STL store no units at all, so the program has to guess.

Hence the classic “the model arrived 1000 times too big”.
cards/3/body:
In some programs up is the Y axis (glTF, Maya, Unity); in others it is Z (Blender, 3ds Max, Unreal Engine, most CAD systems).

If you do not rotate the model on export, it will lie on its side.
cards/4/task: A 10 cm mug is exported without conversion from a Z-up program into a glTF viewer. Pick the settings so the mug stands upright at a normal size.
cards/5/q: A 25 mm part was exported in inches (0.984). The slicer assumed the STL is in millimeters. What size will it show?
cards/5/explain: STL stores no units. The slicer read 0.984 as millimeters, and the part became tiny.
cards/6/q: Why do the wheels move with the car when you move it?
cards/6/options/0: The wheels are child nodes: their transform is relative to the parent
cards/6/options/1: The program moves every object in the scene
cards/6/options/2: The wheels are merged with the body into one mesh
cards/6/explain: The wheel’s final position = the car’s transform × the body’s × the wheel’s own.
cards/7/q: Which of these use Y up? Select all.
cards/7/explain: Blender, 3ds Max and Unreal are Z up. Exporters usually rotate the model for you, but not always.
